p.src: There were many things in Tokyo that astonished Sanshirō. First, he was startled by the clanging bells of the streetcars. Then he was amazed at the tremendous number of people getting on and off while the bells went on clanging. Next, Marunouchi astonished him. What astonished him most was that no matter how far he went, Tokyo never came to an end. And wherever and however he walked, timber lay strewn about, stones stood in piles, new houses sat several yards back from the street, and old storehouses, half demolished, remained forlornly at the front. Everything seemed to be in the process of destruction. And at the same time, everything seemed to be in the process of construction. The movement was tremendous. Sanshirō was utterly astonished. In short, he was every bit as overwhelmed, in both degree and kind, as any ordinary country boy standing in the heart of the capital for the first time. All his learning up to then had proved less effective than a patent medicine in guarding him against this shock. Along with this astonishment, Sanshirō's confidence diminished by roughly forty percent. It was unbearably unpleasant. If this furious activity was itself the real world, then the life he had led until now had never touched the real world in the slightest. It was as though he had been napping at Horagatōge. But even if he stopped napping as of today, it would be difficult to say whether he could shoulder his share of all this activity. I now stand at the center of all this activity. Yet all that has changed is that I have been placed in a position where I must watch the activity occurring all around me; my life as a student remains no different from before. The world moves and trembles in this way. I watch this upheaval. But I cannot take part in it. My world and the real world lie side by side on the same plane, yet they touch nowhere.

p.src: Standing in the heart of Tokyo and watching the movement of streetcars and trains, of people in white clothes and people in black, Sanshirō felt all this. Yet he was wholly unaware of the intellectual activity unfolding behind the surface of student life. —Meiji thought was repeating in forty years three centuries of activity manifested in the history of the West. While Sanshirō remained shut up in the midst of restless Tokyo, brooding alone, a letter arrived from his mother back home. It was the first thing he had received in Tokyo. When he looked, he found all sorts of things written in it. It began with the happy news that this year's harvest was abundant, then warned him to take care of his health, cautioned him that everyone in Tokyo was clever and unscrupulous, assured him that his school expenses would arrive at the end of every month, and concluded by saying that a cousin of Masa from Katsuta had graduated from the university and was apparently attached to the College of Science or some such place, so Sanshirō ought to seek him out and ask for his help in all matters. Apparently she had forgotten the all-important name, for in what amounted to the margin she had written, “Mr. Sōhachi Nonomiya.” There were two or three other items in this margin. Saku's roan horse had died suddenly of illness, leaving Saku in terrible distress. Omitsu of Miwada had given them some sweetfish, but because they would have spoiled on the way if sent to Tokyo, the family had eaten them instead, and so on. Reading this letter, Sanshirō somehow felt as though it had reached him from a faded, bygone age. He even thought, with apologies to his mother, that he had no time to read such things. Nevertheless, he read it twice over. In short, if he had any contact at all with the real world, for the present it was probably through no one but his mother. And his mother was an old-fashioned person living in an old-fashioned countryside. Besides her, there was the woman who had shared his railway carriage. She was a flash of lightning from the real world.

p.src: The next day was hotter than usual. Since it was vacation, he doubted that Nonomiya would be at the College of Science even if he went looking for him there; but as his mother had not told him where Nonomiya lodged, he decided to go and make inquiries at the same time, and at about four in the afternoon he passed beside the Higher School and entered through the gate at Yayoi-chō. The road was covered with nearly two inches of dust, in which the teeth of wooden clogs, the soles of shoes, and the undersides of straw sandals were all perfectly imprinted. There was no telling how many tracks had been left by carriage wheels and bicycles. The road was unbearably stifling, but once he entered the campus, the abundance of trees made him feel refreshed, as one might expect. He tried the first door he came to and found it locked. Going around to the back was no use either. At last he went around to the side. Thinking he might as well make sure, he pushed at the door, and luckily it opened. At a junction in the corridor, a janitor sat dozing. When Sanshirō explained his business, the man spent a while gazing toward the woods of Ueno as if trying to recover his senses, then suddenly said, “He may be here,” and went farther inside. It was exceedingly quiet. Before long, the man came back. “He’s here. Come on in,” he said, as familiarly as if they were friends. Following close behind the janitor, Sanshirō turned a corner and descended along a corridor with an earthen floor. The whole world suddenly went dark. It was like being dazzled by the blazing sun, but after a while his eyes finally adjusted and he could see his surroundings. Being underground, it was relatively cool. There was a door on the left, standing wide open. A face appeared in the doorway. With his broad forehead and large eyes, he had the look of a man somehow connected with Buddhism. He wore a suit jacket over a crêpe shirt, and the jacket was stained here and there. He was extremely tall. His thinness seemed well suited to the heat. He thrust his head and back forward in a straight line and bowed.

p.src: Saying only, “This way,” he withdrew his face into the room. Sanshirō came up to the doorway and peered into the room. Nonomiya was already seated in a chair. Once more he said, “This way.” Where he was indicating stood a platform. It consisted of four square posts with boards laid across the top. Sanshirō sat down on the platform and offered the customary greetings for a first meeting. Then he asked Nonomiya to kindly look after him. Nonomiya merely listened, responding, “Yes, yes.” His manner somewhat resembled that of the man who had eaten the honey peach on the train. Having delivered his prepared remarks, Sanshirō found he had nothing more to say. Nonomiya, too, stopped saying, “Yes, yes.”

p.src: Looking around the room, he saw a large, long oak table standing in the middle. On it sat some sort of intricate apparatus bristling with thick wires, and beside it stood a large glass bowl filled with water. There were also a file, a knife, and a necktie lying there. Finally, looking into the far corner, he saw an intricate apparatus about the size of a can of fukujinzuke set atop a granite pedestal roughly three feet high. Sanshirō noticed two holes in the side of this canlike apparatus. The holes gleamed like the eyes of a python. Nonomiya smiled and said, “They shine, don’t they?” Then he gave the following explanation. “We make all those preparations during the day, then at night, when traffic and other activity have subsided, we peer through the telescope at those eye-like things here in this quiet, dark cellar. That is how we test the pressure of light. I began around New Year, but the apparatus is so troublesome that I still haven’t obtained the results I want. Summer is comparatively bearable, but on cold nights it is extremely hard to endure. Even in an overcoat and scarf, the cold is unbearable. …” Sanshirō was greatly astonished. Astonished as he was, he also found it utterly impossible to grasp what sort of pressure light could exert or what use such pressure might have. At that point Nonomiya urged Sanshirō, “Take a look.” Half out of curiosity, Sanshirō went over to the telescope standing several yards in front of the stone pedestal and put his right eye to it, but he could see nothing. “Well? Can you see anything?” Nonomiya asked. When Sanshirō answered, “I can’t see a thing,” Nonomiya said, “Ah, I forgot to remove the cap,” rose from his chair, and took off the covering over the end of the telescope.

p.src: When he looked again, he saw ruler-like graduations against a bright field with blurred outlines. The numeral 2 appeared below. Nonomiya asked again, “Well?” When Sanshirō said, “I can see the numeral 2,” Nonomiya replied, “It will move in a moment,” then went around to the other side and appeared to do something there.

p.src: Before long, the graduations began to move across the bright field. The 2 disappeared. Then 3 appeared. After it came 4. Then came 5. At last it reached 10. Then the graduations began moving in the opposite direction. The 10 vanished, then the 9, and the numbers passed successively from 8 to 7, from 7 to 6, until they reached 1 and stopped. Nonomiya again asked, “Well?” Startled, Sanshirō pulled his eye away from the telescope. He no longer even felt like asking what the graduations meant. After offering his courteous thanks, he climbed out of the cellar and emerged where people passed by, only to find the world outside still blazing hot. Though it was hot, he drew a deep breath. The sun, now declining in the west, shone obliquely across the broad slope, and the glass windows of the engineering buildings on either side at its top blazed like fire. The sky was deeply clear, and through that clarity it seemed as though pale-red flames from a fire burning beyond the western horizon were blowing back and casting their heat as far as the space above Sanshirō’s head. With half his back turned to the slanting sunlight, Sanshirō entered the woods on his left. The woods too had half their back turned to the same evening sun. Between the dark bluish leaves, the spaces were red as though dyed. A higurashi cicada was singing on the trunk of a thick zelkova. Sanshirō came to the pond and crouched beside it. It was extraordinarily quiet. There was not even the sound of a streetcar. While still in the provinces, he had read in the newspaper that the streetcar line meant to pass in front of the Red Gate had been diverted through Koishikawa after the university protested. Crouching at the edge of the pond, Sanshirō suddenly recalled the incident. A university that would not even let a streetcar pass must be remarkably removed from society. And when one happened to enter it, one found people like Nonomiya, who had spent more than half a year underground in a cellar testing the pressure of light. Nonomiya dressed extremely simply; encountered outside, he might have passed for a technician from an electric-light company.

Yet however much the scale inside the telescope may move, it plainly has no connection with the real world. Perhaps Nonomiya has no intention of coming into contact with the real world for the rest of his life. In short, breathing this tranquil air must naturally put one into such a frame of mind. p.src: As Sanshirō sat motionless gazing at the surface of the pond, countless great trees were reflected deep in the water, and beneath them he could see the blue sky. At that moment Sanshirō felt himself far away—beyond the streetcars, beyond Tokyo, beyond Japan. But after a while, a loneliness like a thin veil of cloud spread through that feeling and covered it entirely. He felt so desolate that it seemed as though he had entered Nonomiya's cellar and were sitting there all alone. During his days at the high school in Kumamoto, he had often climbed Mount Tatsuta, quieter even than this place, or lain on the athletic field where nothing but evening primroses grew, and felt that he had completely forgotten the world; but never before had he experienced this sense of isolation. Was it because he had seen the feverish activity of Tokyo? Or perhaps—at this thought, Sanshirō blushed. It was because he had remembered the woman who had shared his railway carriage. —It seemed that he did need the real world after all. And yet the real world seemed too dangerous to approach. Sanshirō decided to return to his lodgings soon and write a letter to his mother. Glancing up, he saw two women standing on the hill to his left. Directly below the women lay the pond; on the far side stood a wooded, steep bluff, and beyond that rose a flamboyant red-brick building in the Gothic style. The sinking sun cast its light sideways from beyond them all. The women stood facing the evening sun. Seen from the low shadow where Sanshirō crouched, the hilltop was brilliantly bright. One of the women, apparently dazzled by the light, was holding a round fan above her forehead. He could not make out her face clearly. But the colors of her kimono and sash showed vividly. The white of her tabi socks also caught his eye. He could not tell the color of the sandal straps, but he could see that she was wearing zōri. The other woman was entirely in white. She carried neither a fan nor anything else.

p.src: At that moment, Sanshirō's only impression was of beautiful colors. But being a country boy, he could neither say nor write in what way those colors were beautiful. He merely assumed that the one in white was a nurse. Sanshirō remained lost in admiration. Then the woman in white began to move. She did not move as though she had somewhere to go. It was as though her feet had begun moving of their own accord before she knew it. He looked and saw that the woman with the fan had also begun moving again without his noticing. As if by prior agreement, the two came down the slope with the aimless gait of people who had nowhere to go. Sanshirō continued to watch them. At the foot of the slope was a stone bridge. If they did not cross it, they would go straight toward the College of Science. If they crossed it, they would follow the water's edge and come his way. The two women crossed the stone bridge. The fan was no longer raised as a sunshade. The young woman held a small white flower in her left hand and came along smelling it. As she walked, smelling the flower beneath her nose and gazing at it, her eyes remained lowered. When she came within about six feet of Sanshirō, she suddenly stopped. “What kind of tree is this?” she asked, looking up. Above her stood a great chinquapin, its foliage so dense that no sunlight filtered through, its rounded crown extending all the way over the water's edge. “It's a chinquapin,” said the nurse. She sounded just as though she were teaching a child. “I see. There aren't any nuts on it,” she said, lowering her upturned face again; as she did so, she glanced at Sanshirō. Sanshirō was distinctly conscious of the instant when her dark pupils moved. At that moment, every impression of color vanished, and he encountered something that defied description. That something resembled, in some way, what he had felt when the woman on the train told him, “You aren't a very bold man, are you?” Sanshirō became frightened. The two women passed in front of Sanshirō.

p.src: Sanshirō stood there in a daze. Presently, he murmured, “A contradiction.” Whether the contradiction lay between the atmosphere of the university and that woman, between those colors and that look in her eyes, in the fact that seeing her had reminded him of the woman on the train, in the two conflicting paths of his own plans for the future, or in his feeling fear toward something that delighted him immensely—the young man from the country understood none of it. He only knew that somehow it was a contradiction. Sanshirō picked up the flower the woman had dropped. Then he smelled it. But it had no particular fragrance. Sanshirō threw the flower into the pond. The flower floated on the water. Suddenly, someone on the other side called his name. Sanshirō took his eyes off the flower. He looked and saw Nonomiya standing tall on the far side of the stone bridge. “Are you still here?” Nonomiya said. Before answering, Sanshirō got up and plodded toward him. When he reached the stone bridge, he said, “Yes.” There was something vaguely foolish about him. But Nonomiya showed no surprise at all. “Is it cool here?” he asked. Sanshirō again said, “Yes.” Nonomiya gazed at the pond for a while, then put his right hand into his pocket and searched for something. An envelope protruded halfway from his pocket. The writing on it appeared to be in a woman's hand. Apparently unable to find what he wanted, Nonomiya withdrew his hand as it was and let it hang loosely at his side. Then he said: “The apparatus went slightly out of order today, so I've called off the evening experiment. I thought I would take a walk around Hongō before going home. How about it—would you like to come with me?” Sanshirō readily agreed. Together they climbed the slope and emerged at the top of the hill.

p.src: Nonomiya paused for a moment near where the woman had been standing, and surveyed the red building visible through the blue-green grove beyond, together with the pond below the high bluff, its water drained away. “It is rather a fine view, isn’t it? Only the angled corner of that building projects a little into view. Through the trees. See? Isn’t it fine? Have you noticed it? That building is very skillfully designed. The Engineering building is well done too, but this one is better.” Sanshirō was a little surprised by Nonomiya’s powers of appreciation. The truth was that he himself had no idea which of the two was better. So this time it was Sanshirō who began murmuring, “Yes, yes.”

p.src: “And then there is the feeling of these trees and this water. It is nothing extraordinary, but after all, here we are in the very heart of Tokyo—and yet it is quiet, isn’t it? One needs a place like this to pursue scholarship. Tokyo has grown far too noisy lately; it is quite troublesome. This is the Palace,” he said as he resumed walking and pointed to the building on their left. “It is where the faculty council meets. Oh, it does not matter—I need not attend such things. I need only go on living my life down in the cellar. Scholarship advances with tremendous speed nowadays, and if you relax your attention for even a moment, you are left behind at once. To an observer it may look as though we are merely joking about in a cellar, but the mind of the person doing the work is operating with terrific intensity. It may be working much more furiously than a streetcar. That is why, even in summer, I cannot bear to spend the time traveling,” he said, tilting his head back to gaze at the vast sky. Little sunlight remained in the sky. Across the utterly still surface of the blue sky, thin white clouds floated in long diagonal streaks, like traces left after the tip of a brush had swept over it. “Do you know what that is?” he asked. Sanshirō looked up at the translucent clouds. “Those are all particles of snow. Seen from down here like this, they do not appear to move at all. Yet they are moving faster than a hurricane over the earth. Have you read Ruskin?” Disconcerted, Sanshirō replied that he had not. Nonomiya merely said, “I see.” After a while he said, “It would be interesting to sketch this sky. Perhaps I should mention it to Haraguchi.” Naturally, Sanshirō did not know the name of the painter Haraguchi. From the statue of Baelz, the two men passed beside Karatachi Temple and came out onto the streetcar avenue. In front of the statue, Nonomiya asked him what he thought of it, and Sanshirō was at a loss once again.

p.src: Outside, the street was extremely lively. Streetcars passed without cease.

p.src: “Don’t you find the streetcars noisy?” he asked again. To Sanshirō, they were not merely noisy but positively deafening. But he merely answered, “Yes.” Then Nonomiya said, “I find them noisy too.” Yet he did not look bothered by the noise in the least. “Unless a conductor tells me how, I can’t manage the transfers freely on my own. There have been so many new lines added in the last two or three years, you see. They’ve made things more convenient, and that only makes them more troublesome. It’s just like my field of study,” he said with a laugh. As the term was just beginning, quite a few students wearing the caps of their new higher schools passed by. Nonomiya watched them with evident pleasure. “A good many newcomers have arrived,” he said. “It’s good to see the energy young people have. By the way, how old are you?” he asked. Sanshirō gave the same age he had written in the inn register. “Then you’re about seven years younger than I am. A man can accomplish almost anything in seven years. But time passes quickly, you know. Seven years will be gone before you know it,” he said. Sanshirō could not tell which of the two assertions was true. As they approached the intersection, they saw many bookshops and magazine stalls on both sides of the street. At two or three of them, people crowded thick as a swarm, reading the magazines. Then they went away without buying anything. “They’re a crafty lot,” Nonomiya said, laughing. Though he himself did pick up Taiyō and glance through it. At the intersection, there was a Western-style notions shop on the near side to their left and a Japanese notions shop across the street. Between them, the streetcars swept around the curve at tremendous speed. Their bells clanged and clanged. The crossing was so congested that it was difficult to get across. Pointing to the notions shop across the street, Nonomiya said, “I just need to buy something over there,” and dashed across amid the incessant ringing of the bells.

p.src: Sanshirō stayed close behind him and crossed to the other side. Nonomiya promptly went into the shop. As Sanshirō waited outside, he happened to notice combs, ornamental flower hairpins, and the like arranged in the glass-fronted display case. Sanshirō thought this odd. Wondering suspiciously what Nonomiya could be buying, he went inside and found him dangling a ribbon as delicate as a cicada’s wing and asking, “What do you think?” At that moment, Sanshirō considered buying something himself and sending it to Omitsu of Miwada in thanks for the sweetfish. But he decided against it, thinking that when Omitsu received it, instead of taking it as thanks for the sweetfish, she would surely concoct all sorts of self-serving explanations for it.

p.src: After that, Nonomiya treated him to a Western-style meal in Masagochō. According to Nonomiya, it was the best restaurant in Hongō. To Sanshirō, however, it tasted merely like Western food. Nevertheless, he ate every bit of it. He parted from Nonomiya outside the Western-style restaurant and, on his way back to Oiwake, carefully retraced his steps to the same intersection before turning left. Thinking of buying a pair of wooden clogs, he peered into a clog shop, but beneath an incandescent gaslight sat a girl with her face freshly painted stark white, like some plaster monster; he was suddenly repelled and gave up the idea. For the rest of the way home, he thought only of the complexion of the woman he had met beside the university pond. —It was a tawny shade, like the faintly browned surface of toasted rice cake. And the texture of her skin was extraordinarily fine. Sanshirō concluded that no other complexion would do for a woman.
